newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Germany's wealthy churches worry about tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Germany's wealthy churches worry about tax cuts.

text.p: German taxpayers sang "hallelujah" when they heard the government promise to cut income tax but the response from Germany's churches was more like "Heaven help us."
At first glance, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's plan to reduce income taxes dramatically in 1999 should be one of the most popular decisions he could make.

But the wealthy Roman Catholic and Protestant churches get most of their funds through a church tax linked to believers' income tax returns and a drop in the latter threatens to crimp their declining finances.

The looming cuts worry church leaders, whose organisations provide a vast array of care and educational services as part of Germany's generous social system, but they are wary about taking to the pulpits to denounce them too loudly.

"We support the basic goal of tax reform, but not everything about tax reform," said Heike Thome, a spokeswoman for the German Conference of Bishops, the country's Catholic church organisation. "The church won't be able to replace this money from other sources."

There is little sympathy for the churches' plight outside the shrinking circle of regular churchgoers. Many Germans believe the Catholic and Protestant churches are wealthy enough to absorb a 10 to 20 percent cut in the 17 billion marks ($11.1 billion) Bonn funnels to them each year.

"Those taxes annoy a lot of people because the churches don't need so much money," said Margot Oehlerking, who pays more than 100 marks a month as a Catholic, although she rarely attends mass. "Where I work we make profits but still look in every corner to save money. Churches should have to save, too."

Germany's 28.5 million Protestants and 28 million Catholics pay an extra sum -- eight or nine percent of the income tax they owe -- as church taxes. In 1995 the levies brought in 8.3 billion marks for the EKD, the main Protestant church group, and 8.4 billion for Germany's Roman Catholic Church.
If Kohl keeps his pledge to cut Germany's hefty income tax load by 20 to 30 billion marks in 1999, the churches' take will also fall -- by 10 to 20 percent.

Even some theologians say people like Oehlerking are right. "These are the richest churches in the world," Heidelberg University's Gerhard Besier told Reuters. "The churches have great bureaucracies. Tax reform is a chance to reform them."
Indeed, thanks to the taxes, the churches boast heavier balance sheets than some top corporations.

With taxes providing 90 percent of their revenue, the churches had budgets that made each of them twice as large as Adidas, the German sports shoe company, which had 1995 revenues of 4.9 billion marks.

Despite the size of their budgets, the two churches hint tax reform might force them to curtail some services provided by the thousands of nursing homes and other care centres they run -- and possibly leave the state to pick up the slack.

"We hope we won't have to close hospitals or kindergartens, but, if it gets to that point, the state may have to take over and then all taxpayers will pay for them," said EKD spokesman Hannes Schoeb in Hanover.
Heidelberg's Besier said the churches exaggerated the danger. Most of the social services are subsidised by some six billion marks from state governments annually, not the church tax, he said.
"The church tax doesn't pay for the hospitals and schools. That is something few people know and the churches don't like to talk about it."

Church taxes help preserve bloated bureaucracies, Besier argued. "The EKD has 24 separate state administrations that could be dismantled, but the officials don't want to give up their positions or their power," he said.

Besier said the churches also had vast unused resources: "They own giant tracts of forest that could bring great amounts of capital they could invest in world markets. Like the rest of society, they now have to work differently, economically."
Anyway, dwindling membership may pose a greater threat to church finances than tax reform. Each church is losing 150,000 to 250,000 members per year, many just to dodge the extra tax.

"I'm thinking about getting out because money's tight," said Michael Reichert, a Protestant father of three. "We don't go to church or use the church kindergarten, so we don't see where the money goes."
He said he hasn't left yet because it is time-consuming and a bit embarrassing to fill out the forms at the tax office.

The recent drive for tax reform has put the politically powerful churches on the defensive. Their leaders meet with Kohl's cabinet periodically but have refrained from speaking out loudly as they have against Bonn's welfare cuts.
"The will is toward a slimmer, trimmer state," said Hans-Guenter Roehrig, a spokesman for the Bamberg archdiocese. "The state savings must go on, so the church has to save, too."

Their main hope now is to keep the deductibility of church taxes, which are taken out before taxable income is calculated. The coalition has proposed lowering the top tax rate to 35 percent from 53 percent, but deductibility is undecided.
"It is improbable it will go away," said Uwe Evers, a spokesman for Kohl's Free Democrat coalition partners. "But in the future everyone must pay less taxes." ($1=1.5330 Mark)
